1: amnis … obsite: the vocative perfect passive participle (from obserere) marks the river as the addressee. Compare the opening address of the guard (ianitor) in Amores 1.6.1. limosas … ripas: an accusative specifying in what respect the river is covered with reeds (A&G 397b).
2: propero: the first-person speaker succinctly states his objective. siste: “check the flow of” (OLD s.v. sisto 7). parumper: the adverb construes the favor being asked as a relatively small one.
3: The speaker details his plight: this river has no bridges and no hand-pulled rope ferry. tibi: dative of possession (A&G 373). quae: the antecedent cumba appears within the relative clause (and in the next verse). A rendering in English word order might yield the following: nec (est) concaua cumba quae uehat traiecto rudente (et) sine ictu remigis.
4: traiecto … rudente: “by means of a rope having been crossed” (cf. OLD s.v. traicio 7).
5: The speaker recalls a prior encounter with this river. nec te transire refugi: “I did not avoid crossing you”
6: unda: not a “wave” but the river’s “water” in general.
7: The speaker provides additional temporal and spatial details about the setting. Snow is melting from nearby mountains. solutis: “melted” (OLD s.v. soluo 13).
8: The vocabulary underscores the river’s new depth and turbidity.
9: quid … iuuat: “what does it profit” or, more colloquially, “what’s the point of.” Ovid routinely pairs this interrogative clause with an infinitive, as here with properasse, dedisse, and conseruisse. (Cf. Amores 2.6.19, 2.11a.13, and 2.14.1) The verb iuuat is not repeated, but the interrogative quid is. properasse = properauisse
10: tempora: modified by parca in the previous verse. nocti conseruisse diem: a modern idiom for “to have joined day to night” could be “to have pulled an all-nighter.”
11: si: two protases retroactively frame the previous couplet as a compound apodosis within a conditional sentence. hic: adverbial meaning “here” standum est: a passive periphrastic used impersonally (A&G 500.3). datur: the verb’s subject ripa arrives midway through the next verse.
12: premenda: scansion shows that this future passive participle modifies ulterior … ripa. English might prefer an indirect statement for expressing the second protasis, e.g., “…if it’s not granted through any skills that the further shore is to be pressed by our feet.”
13: In this and the following couplet, the speaker offers two mythological references, the first to Perseus (a descendent of Danaë) and the second to Triptolemus (the inventor of agriculture who piloted a flying chariot gifted by Ceres/Demeter). Both shared an ability to fly. ego: the verb for which this serves as subject (opto) doesn’t appear until v. 15. pinnas: the antecedent of quas is in the relative clause, but the relative pronoun can also be translated as an adjective, e.g., “what wings.” Danaēius: this matronymic specifying a male “descendent of Danaë” refers to Perseus and scans as five syllables, with each vowel getting its own syllable. The e is long by nature.
14: angue: ablative of specification (A&G 418) with densum. The reference is to Medusa’s decapitated head.
15: optō: the verb retroactively completes the sense of vv. 13-14 while functioning within its own couplet. currum: the chariot of Triptolemus, a gift from Ceres/Demeter, was pulled by flying serpents or dragons. The speaker makes no mention of flight or even Triptolemus, relying instead on the river’s (and readers’) knowledge of the mythological origins of agriculture. (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/64/Triptolemos_Kore_Louvre_G452_full.jpg) Cerealia: relating to Ceres, whose name is a frequent metonym for “wheat” (OLD s.v. Cerealis 2).
16: in rude missa solum: note the graphic word order. The seeds have been sent into the wild soil.
17: prodigiosa: Kenney punctuates this verse with a comma between loquor and ueterum, construing this as a neuter plural substantive adjective. Alternatively, one may read it as an adjective modifying mendacia. ueterum mendacia uatum: the speaker of Amores 3.12 dwells at length (vv. 19-42) on the limits of poetic license. While the speaker of 3.6 doesn’t explicitly identify as a poet, he seems to be aware of poetic powers and pitfalls and to participate in the topos of raising the fallibility of poets.
18: haec: the direct object of both tulit and feret. The sense of the verb (in both tenses) is “to bring about” or “to produce” (cf. OLD s.v. ferō 23 and 24), although 30d cites this precise verse beneath the definition “(of time) to bring with it” (situations, etc.)”. The use of the same verb in multiple tenses also occurs in claims of prophetic powers (e.g., Apollo’s boast in Met. 1.517-8: per me, quod eritque fuitque / estque, patet).
19: effuse: as in the opening verse, a vocative perfect passive participle modifies amnis.
20: sic aeternus eas: in trying to ingratiate himself with the river, the speaker wishes it a perpetual course. This aside is recalled (and reframed) in v. 98. labere fine tuo: “glide on within your bounds.” labere is the singular present imperative of the deponent verb labor, labī.
21: The speaker pivots rapidly from diplomacy to threat, a foreshadowing of the final section of the poem. inuidiae: the dative of purpose can be translated as “a source of ill-will.” ferendae: the future passive participle (literally “about to be endured”) carries the sense of “endurable” or “tolerable.”
22: per te: “on account of you” A modern editor might put retentus amans in quotations marks. Because the speaker is the only person present, he is not concerned about his reputation as much as about what the designation would say about his actual circumstances.
23: The speaker lays the groundwork for a catalog of mythological “loves” of—and, on occasion, rapes perpetrated by—various rivers to be recounted throughout the next 20 verses.
24: As with Nape in Amores 1.11 and Ceres in Amores 3.10, the elegiac speaker attempts to persuade his interlocutor by suggesting a shared familiarity with the experience of love. esset: subjunctive in an indirect question.
25: The commentaries by Davis (2023) and McKeown and Littlewood (2023) provide admirable detail about Ovid’s potential sources and the personnel involved in the affairs in these two- and four-verse vignettes. The goal of the present notes is to ease grammatical comprehension rather than provide explanation of the various myths. Modern readers do well to recall, first, that some of speaker’s allusions are extremely recondite and, second, that the speaker’s objective is to inundate (pardon the pun) the river with examples. Inachus: a river god who was also the first king of Argos (a polis on the Greek Peloponnese) and the father of Io. Kenney prints the Greek nominative Inachos in his OCT, but this form doesn’t seem to appear in any of the oldest manuscripts. in: “in the case of” (followed by an ablative). Cf. OLD s.v. in 42) Melie Bithynide: ablatives designating a nymph named Melia (or Melie) from Bithynia, a region just south of the Black Sea.
26: dicitur: complemented by isse in previous verse and incaluisse later in this one. incaluisse: “to have grown warm” (with love or passion).
27: fuit … obsessa = erat obsessa lustris … duobus: referring to the famed, ten-year length of the Trojan war as two lustra, or five-year periods.
28: Xanthe: vocative of Xanthus, a river near Troy also known as the Scamander. rapuit: that a woman did the “snatching” or “stealing” inverts gendered expectations. uultus … tuos = “your attentions” Neaera: nominative. Numerous mythological women have this name.
29: Alpheon: an accusative (showing Greek endings) of Alpheus, a river who attempted to rape the Arcadian nymph Arethusa, pursuing her through various lands. Arcadia is a region on the Greek Peloponnese, but Ovid has Arethusa recount a version in her own words in Metamorphoses 5.487-641 in which she ultimately emerges, following Alpheus’s pursuit, as a spring in Sicily.
31: A rendering of the couplet in English word order might yield the following: ferunt te, Penee, quoque occuluisse Creusam promissam Xutho terris Pthiotum. The word order as it appears, with four proper names recited in sequence across the enjambment, seems deliberately difficult. Xutho: dative of Xuthus, the husband of a woman named Creusa. Manuscripts read Xantho, but conflation of the names seems reasonable enough following Xanthus’s naming in v. 28. Penee: vocative of Peneus. A river god by the same name appears as the father of Daphne in Metamorphoses 1.452-552. The vocative retroactively construes the te at the beginning of the verse as designating Peneus rather than agreeing with promissam. Creusam: accusative of Creusa. Numerous mythological women by this name are attested; Ovid may be conflating multiple of them.
32: Pthiotum: genitive plural of Pthiotae (perhaps a contraction of Pthiotarum; see McKeown and Littlewood (2003) ad loc.). The manuscripts are far from certain about this word. occuluisse: the accusative direct object appears in the previous verse. ferunt: a potential “Alexandrian footnote” by which the speaker (or Ovid) acknowledges a debt to another mythological tradition.
33: Asopon: accusative of Asopus, a river near Thebes in northern Attica. Martia Thebe: nominatives designating “Thebe related to Mars,” where “Thebe” is a woman’s name. Her connection to Mars derive from an association between her “hometown” of Thebes and the god of war.
34: In offering more details about Thebe, the verse alludes to the aftermath of the relationship between Thebe and Asopus. quinque: cardinal numbers above four are indeclinable, but context demands that this word modify natarum.
35: Not only is the indirect question placed before the verb that introduces it, but the interrogative introducing the indirect question is postponed. A rendering of this verse in English word order might yield the following: si requiram ubi sint tua cornua nunc, Acheloe […]. cornua: the river god Achelous had the ability to change his shape. While in the form of a bull, he fought Hercules for the right to marry Deianira, but the hero defeated him and broke off one of his horns. In Achelous’s own telling in Ovid’s Metamorphoses 1.1-97, nymphs transformed his broken horn into a cornucopia. Acheloe: vocative of Achelous, a river in western Greece.
36: Herculis: genitive of Hercules. irata: scansion shows that this modifies manu. fracta: an implied esse (or fuisse) makes this the infinitive in an indirect statement introduced by querere. The accusative subject is cornua in v. 35. querere: scansion shows this to be a future indicative verb (querēre) and the conditional sentence to be future more vivid (A&G 516a).
37: tanti: “of such great value” (A&G 417). The repetition of this word hammers focalizes the Achelous’s desire for Deianira. Calydon: a city in Aetolia Aetolia: a region in western Greece along whose border the Achelous river runs
38: Deianira: nominative. She became the wife of Hercules after he and Achelous fought.
39: septena: the Nile was famed for having seven branches, or “mouths” (ostia). Nilus: nominative for the Nile.
40: A reference to the unknown source of the Nile.
41: Manuscript uncertainty plagues the interpretation of the proper names in this verse, but whoever was the object of the Nile’s affection, his abundant waters were unable to quench the flame of his love for her. fertur: “is said.” The subject is Nilus, v. 39. in Euanthe … Asopide: “in the case of Evanthe, daughter of Asopis.” For this use of in, see the note on v. 25. Asopide: an ablative (nominative = Asopis) designating a child of Asopis.
42: uincere: complementary infinitive with (non) potuisse, which itself is complementary with fertur (v. 41).
43: siccus: “when dry.” The adjective is proleptic, anticipating Enipeus’s state after he has ordered the waters to recede. ut: the purpose clause appears before the independent clause. amplecti: present deponent infinitive. Salmonida: accusative of the patronym Salmonis. The daughter of Salmoneus is Tyro, whose rape by Poseidon is recounted in Odyssey 11.235-54. Enipeus: a river in Thessaly, a region in central Greece.
45: The speaker embarks upon an extended narrative, namely, the tale of the river Aniene (Anien, Anienis in Latin; a tributary of the Tiber) and Ilia, which continues for 38 verses.
46: Tiburis Argei: genitives meaning “of Argive Tibur.” Tibur (note the difference in vowel from “Tiber”) is modern-day Tivoli. Horace’s Odes 2.6.5 declares in passing that Tibur was settled by an Argive farmer. pomifer: Manuscripts P, Y, and S all contain pomifer, although the primary scribe of Y attached the first a in arua to pomifer, and only a correcting hand in different ink suggested reattaching it to -rua. Davis (2023) makes a strong stylistic case for reading pomifera, namely, that arua otherwise lacks a modifier.
47: Ilia: nominative. This alternative name for Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus and Remus, emphasizes her ties to Ilium, or Troy. cultu: ablative of specification (A&G 418).
48: The symmetry of this verse calls to mind the raking of fingernails down each side of a face. comas: an accusative of specification (A&G 397b) “used to denote the part affected.”
49: Ilia is grieving for two reasons: a crime (nefas) of her uncle Amulius (perhaps the exposure of her twins) and the crimes (delicta) of Mars (presumably her rape). The polysyndeton (i.e., unnecessary repetition of -que) emphasizes the multiple causes of her lamentation. She soon articulates another reason: she has lost her status as a Vestal Virgin through no fault of her own.
51: Anien: nominative. The name also appears as Anio in the nominative.
52: rauca: the adjective (modifying ora) is striking, applying a sonic descriptor to something visual. The noun os can refer to a face or a voice, but Anien’s action suggests the raising of his features from water’s surface.
53: Anien already knows who Ilia is, including the fact that she is (was?) a Vestal virgin, but he does not seem to know why she is grieving. anxia: modifying Ilia, the implied subject of teris. Translate adverbially.
54: Ilia: vocative. genus: “offspring” (OLD s.v. genus 2). Read in apposition with Ilia. ab Idaeo Laomedonte: “from Idaean Laomedon.” Laomedon was the mythical founder of Troy, and Idaeus invokes Mt. Ida, a famed mountain near Troy.
55: cultus … tui: her general “self-care” and the garb of a Vestal Virgin, as specified by uitta … alba in v. 56. abiere = synopated form of abierunt.
56: uitta: a headband associated with either matrons or unmarried (presumably virginal) women. Because of her rape, Ilia is neither.
58: Scansion shows that pectora is modified by aperta and insana modifies manu. aperta: Ilia presumably strikes her bared chest.
59: In criticizing the man who would not be moved by the sight of such a woman, Anien indirectly congratulates himself. uiuum … ferrum: living iron.
61: Ilia, pone metus: the framing of the couplet with these words establishes a brief refrain as Anien seems to be attempting to talk Ilia down.
65: Troiana propago: Anien again emphasizes Ilia’s Trojan heritage.
66: promissis: ablative of comparison (A&G 406). Anien assures Ilia of gifts greater than those promised if she does not reject his love.
67: oculos … modestos: accusative of specification (A&G 397b). A smoother translation is possible when deiecta is translated actively.
68: teneros: Manuscripts P and Y both read teneros, an adjective that would modify sinus. A second hand in Y offers tepido, which is the only reading preserved in S and would have to modify imbre. flebilis: scansion shows the final i to be short. This adjective is best read as modifying illa. imbre: “with a stream of tears” (OLD s.v. imber 3a).
69: molita: the perfect participle of the deponent moliri, here modifying an implied Ilia, is translated actively. restitit: “she stayed put” (OLD s.v. restō 1).
70: currendi: take the genitive gerund with uires, the object of eripiente. metu: despite Anien’s urgings in vv. 61-2, Ilia’s fear remains present.
71: sera: the adjective can be read adverbially (i.e., “late”) with edidit. Adding tamen, the sense seems to be, “She produced, albeit late, unworthy sounds […].”
72: Ilia wishes to have died before recent events transpired. A rendering of the couplet in English word order might yield the following: o utinam mea ossa lecta forent conditaque (forent) patrio sepulcro, cum ossa uirginis poterant legi. utinam: marks an optative subjunctive (A&G 442). The pluperfect (lecta forent = lecta essent) indicates that this is an unaccomplished wish for the past. lecta forent: the subject ossa is postponed to late in the following verse and reused in the cum clause as the subject of poterant.
73: condita: resupply forent from the previous verse. Note the repetition forms of legi (i.e., lecta) in this couplet.
74: modo: refers to time just passed, e.g., “until a moment ago.”
75: taedas: wedding torches are metonyms for marriages.
76: Iliacis … focis: “by the hearths of Ilium.” In referring to the eternal flame of Vesta tended by Vestal Virgins, Ilia stresses her new unsuitability for the role. infitianda: “about to be disowned.”
77: designor: Ilia is particularly attuned to her reputation. Compare Tragedy’s critique of the poet-speaker’s reputation in Amores 3.1.19: saepe aliquis digito uatem designat euntem.
78: The word order is challenging. A rendering of the verse in English word order might yield the following: ora quae famosus pudor notet desint. desint: a jussive subjunctive (see A&G 439n2). The sense is, “Let them be absent” or, more pointedly, “Let them perish.” famosus: “infamous” (OLD s.v. famosus 2).
79: hactenus: a verb such as dixit is implied. The sense is that Ilia stopped speaking. Cf. Amores 3.1.31. tumidis … ocellis: dative with praetendit.
80: perdita: “hopeless” (OLD s.v. perditus 2). The adjective appears within the “swift waters.”
81: Anien swiftly prevents Ilia’s attempt to kill herself. supposuisse: dicitur, which introduces this infinitive and dedisse in v. 82, appears at the beginning of the next verse. ad pectora: the phrase is not inherently erotic, but lubricus (i.e., “slippery” or “deceitful”) casts a shadow. The river’s touching of Ilia is doubtless nonconsensual: rape is implied.
82: socii iura … tori: Anien is also said to have given Ilia marriage rights.
83: The speaker restates his belief—or his hope—that the river has once loved a woman. credibile est: one may comfortably render these words as introducing indirect statement (e.g., “it’s believable that…”). Strictly speaking, the presence of est suggests caluisse is a subject infinitive with te as its accusative subject (A&G 452). aliqua … puella: scansion shows these words to be ablative.
84: crimina: the speaker construes whatever action the river took as illicit. tegunt: an implicit explanation for why the speaker may not be familiar with what the river has done.
85: The final phase of the poem has the speaker realizing that the river before him has only swollen during his address. Abandoning any attempt to persuade it, he shifts to insult. increuit: the growth of the river is described in the third person (cf. capit in v. 86), as if the speaker is offering an incredulous aside during his address of the river.
86: admissas … aquas: perhaps caused by the snowmelt of vv. 7-8. alueus: the river channel does not contain the waters.
87: The speaker resumes his direct address (note the vocative furiose) of the river. quid mecum … tibi: a finite form of esse is implied. The sense is “What are you doing with me?” or “What do you want with me?” A similar construction—with a similar note of incredulity—appears in Amores 3.8.49. The speaker is taking matters personally. mutua … gaudia: the shared pleasures of sex. The speaker hints that the river is also punishing his puella.
88: rustice: a vocative insult. The river is uncultured.
89: The speaker imagines how things would be different if the river had a reputation to uphold. legitimum: modifying an implied flumen. flueres: imperfect subjunctive in the protasis of a present contrafactual conditional? The apodosis is implied after quid: “What (would be happening) […]?” si nobile flumen: flueres may be resupplied, or esses, would be imlied.
91: riuis collecte caducis: the vocative phrase presents the river as an accident of drainage rather than an established body of water.
92: tibi … tibi: more datives of possession (A&G 373). The punchy repetition underscores the speaker’s anger.
93: fontis: contrast the singular with the plural fontes in v. 92. niuesque solutas: recalls niuibus … solutis in v. 7.
94: pigra: the adjective is derogatory. The river only exists because of gifts granted by a sluggish winter. It remains a product of chance.
95: aut … aut: the two extremes described in the couplet (lutulentus and puluerentus; neither is desirable and both can be rendered adverbially) cast the river as inconstant.
97: The speaker imagines that the river, owing to its fickleness, is incapable of ever having slaked a traveler’s thirst. potuit: translate with completed aspect, i.e., “has been able to.”
98: quis dixit grata uoce “perennis eas”?: the speaker offered a variation on this wish (aeternus eas) in v. 20, but grata uoce may be doing the heavy lifting here. Perhaps teh speaker is retroactively confessing his insincerity.
99: pecori … agris: datives of reference (or disadvantage; cf. A&G 376) with damnosus and damnosior.
100: alios, me: The speaker shamelessly juxtaposes the concerns of others with his own grievances.
101: The speaker scolds himself for wasting his narrative efforts on the river. huic: the demonstrative suggests an aside rather ongoing speech to the river.
102: iactasse = iactauisse nomina tanta: all the named rivers appearing earlier in the poem. pudet: generally impersonal, but the infinitive can be read as the subject. The person feeling the shame is, of course, the speaker.
103: nescioquem hunc: “this no-name,” object of the participle spectans. Acheloon et Inachon amnem: objects of referre in v. 104. Acheloon is an accusative (with Greek endings) of Achelous (see v. 35). Inachon is an accusative (with Greek endings) of Inachus (see v. 25).
105: pro meritis: “in accordance with your deserts” non candide: the river is muddy.
106: sint: following opto (v. 105), one might expect an ut to introduce the indirect command. rapidi soles: assuming the speaker is wishing the river ill, these “scorching suns” (OLD s.v. rapidus 3) would make the river small in summer.
